passages.t: The call to Nineveh, and the flight to Tarshish
passages.happening:
‘Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai’ (verse 1). He is to get up and go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, ‘because its wickedness has come up before Me’ (verse 2).

‘Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD’ (verse 3). He goes down to Joppa, finds a ship bound for Tarshish, pays the fare and goes aboard, away from the presence of the LORD.
passages.hearers:
The story is set in the eighth century BC, during or near the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel. Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris in what is now northern Iraq, was the great power of the age and was known for its harsh treatment of conquered peoples. Nineveh, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was one of its main cities, later its capital under Sennacherib around 700 BC.

Joppa, modern Jaffa, was one of the few natural harbors on Israel's coast, often under Philistine or Phoenician control. Tarshish lay far to the west, often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, and it stood in Israel's imagination for the far edge of the sea. Nineveh was about 500 miles northeast of Israel; Tarshish was more than 2,000 miles west. Jonah chose the farthest place he could reach.

The phrase away from the presence of the LORD comes twice in one verse. Jonah does not say why he runs until chapter 4.
passages.later: Second Kings names Jonah son of Amittai as ‘the prophet from Gath-hepher’ (2 Kings 14:25). Tarshish stood for the distant coastlands (Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 66:19).
passages.hard:
Why would a prophet try to run away from God, and can anyone really flee his presence?

Jonah surely knew the psalm's confession that no one can escape God's presence. Many interpreters think away from the presence of the LORD means away from God's service, as a servant leaves the presence of the king who commands him, or away from the land where the LORD was specially present in his temple. Jonah's reason is held back until 4:2: he knew God was merciful and did not want Nineveh spared. Some readers add patriotic motives, since Assyria threatened Israel. Others suggest that Jonah feared being seen as a false prophet if Nineveh were spared.

The chapter's point is that flight fails. The God Jonah runs from is the Lord of the sea he runs across.
passages.asks: Jonah ran from a task he did not want. Ask what God has asked of you that you have been sailing away from. And ask whether your reasons for running are the ones you would say out loud.

passages.t: The storm, the praying sailors and the sleeping prophet
passages.happening:
‘Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea’ (verse 4), and the ship is in danger of breaking apart. The sailors are afraid, and each cries out to his own god. They throw the cargo overboard. But Jonah has gone down into the lowest part of the ship and fallen into a deep sleep (verse 5). The captain wakes him: why is he sleeping? He should call on his God, and perhaps this God will spare them (verse 6).

The sailors cast lots to find out who is to blame, and the lot falls on Jonah (verse 7). They ask him who he is and where he comes from (verse 8). ‘I am a Hebrew,’ he answers, ‘I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land’ (verse 9). The men are even more afraid. They know he is running from the LORD, because he has told them (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Ancient sailors, often from several nations, each prayed to his own god in a crisis, because gods were widely believed to rule particular peoples, lands or forces of nature. A storm of unusual violence suggested that some god was angry, so the crew cast lots to find out who was responsible. Lots were small stones or marked objects drawn or thrown; Israel also used them to discern God's will. The sailors' questions, your work, your country, your people, were the natural way to find out which god might be involved.

Jonah's answer terrifies them because he names a God who made the sea and the dry land. A god of one country might be escaped by leaving it. A God who made the sea cannot be escaped on the sea. For the peoples of that world the sea was a place of chaos and danger, and a God who rules it is above all others.

The irony is sharp. The pagan captain has to tell the prophet to pray.
passages.later: Israel also cast lots to learn God's will: ‘The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD’ (Proverbs 16:33). A psalm says the sea is the LORD's, ‘for He made it’ (Psalm 95:5).
passages.asks: The sailors prayed while the prophet slept. Ask whether people outside your faith have sometimes been more alert to God than you. And ask what it would take to wake you up.

passages.t: Thrown into the sea, and a great fish
passages.happening:
The sea grows worse, and the sailors ask what they must do to calm it (verse 11). Jonah says, ‘Pick me up’ and throw him into the sea, ‘For I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you’ (verse 12). The men row hard to get back to land, but they cannot (verse 13). So they cry out to the LORD not to let them die for this man's life, and not to charge them with innocent blood (verse 14). Then they throw Jonah into the sea, ‘and the raging sea grew calm’ (verse 15).

‘Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him’ (verse 16). ‘Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The sailors' reluctance to throw Jonah over, and their prayer not to be held guilty of innocent blood, reflect the common belief that bloodguilt brought punishment from the gods. These men who did not know the LORD behave more honorably than his prophet.

The chapter is built on repetition. The word great marks the great city, the great wind, the sailors' great fear and the great fish. The verb hurl is used of God hurling the wind, the sailors hurling the cargo, and at last the sailors hurling Jonah. And the sailors' fear grows in three stages: fear of the storm, great fear at Jonah's confession, and at last fearing the LORD greatly in worship. The pagan sailors end the chapter worshiping the LORD.

God appoints the fish. In Hebrew Bibles verse 17 is numbered 2:1.
passages.later: Jesus spoke of this verse: ‘For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth’ (Matthew 12:40).
passages.asks: The sailors who threw Jonah into the sea ended up worshiping the God he was running from. Ask how God has used even your failures to bring others near. And ask whose life is in danger because of your disobedience.
